chapter: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
title: Dusty Fletcher's 'Open the Door, Richard' and Stepin Fetchit sightings
summary: Dusty Fletcher did his Richard routine in the Swingland revue; the MC spotted Stepin Fetchit in the house and Fetchit walked out. Horace first saw Fetchit upstaging Bojangles at Connie's Inn.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: He was in this revue, and he was doing that same act that he became famous later on by -- right in Swingland. Open the Door, Richard." And I remember distinctly one night we had a visitor sitting right at the door. The place was packed on Saturday night, and the MC, whose name was Rubel Blakely -- that just came to me. He was quite a guy, and he happened to recognize this particular guy in the audience, sitting near the door. You know who this guy was? Steppin' Fetchit.

So let me tell you what that guy did. They announced him, and they put the spotlight on him. You know what he did? He got up and turned his back to him and walked out. He was quite a guy. Oh, he was something. He had that lazy look. He became famous by it. And that was the second time that I had run across Steppin' Fetchit. The first
time -- I've got to mention this. Can I take you back to New York?

You know, at one time at Connie's Inn we had Bojangles down there. He was tap dancing, and he was doing such a terrific job, and the audience was real silent. He had done this at Connie's Inn, the band playing. So all of a sudden, the audience began to laugh, and everything, and Bojangles didn't know if something had happened to his uniform or something, you know. And we happened to look over in the corner, and there Stepin' Fetchit slipped on the stage, put a chair out, dropped his head like he was sleepin'. It was a funny thing, and Bojangles looked back and saw that man -- you talk about somethin' goin' on. That was a funny thing. Now that was the first time I'd ever seen Fetchit. Then this Chicago incident was the second time. So I began to form my conclusions about him, you know. He didn't want to be introduced, you know. But getting back to that revue. That was an excellent revue, and it kept the band steadily employed. We stayed there for like two and a half, three years, no change, and we broadcast three and four nights a week. So this was a great thing for me in Chicago.
